title: Every network call can fail, and how
objective: By the end of this lesson you can name what each network call fails with, distinguish an error you should retry from one you should not, and write a client that gives up sensibly instead of hanging.

blocks.text: In a single machine, a failed call usually means a bug. On a network, failure is a normal operating condition: the other end restarts, a cable is unplugged, a firewall changes, a route disappears. The question is never whether calls will fail but which failure this is, and that is decided by the errno value.
The errors worth recognising by name

rows: The machine is reachable; the service is not there
Silent filtering, or the host is gone
The peer aborted an established connection
It crashed, or something in the middle closed it
You wrote to a connection the peer has closed
Routing, or an interface is down
Another instance, or TIME_WAIT without SO_REUSEADDR
Not an error — the non-blocking answer

blocks.title: Two of those are not failures, and treating them as failures is a bug
blocks.text: EAGAIN means 'not yet' and EINTR means 'a signal arrived, try again'. Code that logs an error and drops the connection for either one is broken in a way that only shows under load, when signals and readiness edges are common. Every network program needs both handled explicitly, which is why the read_all and write_all loops in the previous lesson check for them by name.

rows: EACCES — permission will not change by asking again
ETIMEDOUT — with backoff, a bounded number of times
EACCES — a permission problem that will not change
ECONNRESET — usually, if the operation is safe to repeat
EMSGSIZE — the request itself is wrong

blocks.text: That last column matters more than the first. Retrying an error that cannot succeed turns one failure into a loop, and retrying without a limit turns a brief outage into an amplified one — every client hammering a service that is already struggling.
Backoff, and why the randomness is not optional

blocks.caption: Exponential backoff with jitter
lines: int delay_ms = 100;
for (int attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt++) {
if (try_once() == 0) return 0;              /* success */
int jitter = rand() % delay_ms;             /* spread the retries out */
usleep((delay_ms + jitter) * 1000);
return -1;                                       /* give up, and say so */
/* Without the jitter, every client that failed at the same moment retries
at the same moment, and the service is hit by a synchronised wave each
time. The randomness is what breaks that up. */

blocks.text: SIGPIPE: the default that kills servers

Writing to a connection the peer has closed raises SIGPIPE, and its default action is to terminate the process. For a shell pipeline that is useful — it is what stops a producer when the reader exits. For a server it is a disaster: one client disconnecting at the wrong moment ends the whole process.

blocks.caption: The one line every network server needs
lines: signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN);   /* now write() returns -1 with errno EPIPE instead */
/* With this, a disconnecting client becomes an error you handle on one
connection, rather than a signal that ends the program. This is the
same mechanism as the signals lesson in the operating systems course,
met here in the situation it matters most. */

blocks.text: Timeouts: the failure that has no error

The worst network failure is the one where nothing happens. A peer that accepts a connection and then stops responding leaves your program waiting indefinitely, with no error to report. Every network operation therefore needs a bound on how long it may take.

blocks.caption: Two ways to bound a wait
lines: /* Per-socket, and simple: */
struct timeval tv = { .tv_sec = 5, .tv_usec = 0 };
setsockopt(fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_RCVTIMEO, &tv, sizeof tv);
setsockopt(fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_SNDTIMEO, &tv, sizeof tv);
/* read and write now return -1 with EAGAIN after 5 seconds */
/* Or through the readiness mechanism, which fits an event loop: */
int n = epoll_wait(ep, events, 64, 5000);   /* milliseconds */
if (n == 0) { /* nothing became ready in time */ }

blocks.title: A connection that is silent is not the same as one that is closed
blocks.text: A closed connection is reported: read returns 0, or a write fails. A silent one reports nothing at all — the peer may have lost power, or a middlebox may have discarded the connection without telling either side. Without a timeout, a program waits for that forever. This is why long-lived connections send periodic keepalives: not to carry data, but to turn silence into a detectable failure.

items: The call that failed, the errno name, and the peer address — all three, or the log is not actionable
Use strerror(errno) or perror; a bare number sends the reader to a table
Capture errno immediately — the next library call may overwrite it
Do not log EAGAIN and EINTR as errors; they are ordinary control flow
Distinguish 'this connection failed' from 'the server cannot continue' — they need different responses

blocks.title: Produce each failure deliberately
steps: Connect to a port with nothing listening and print strerror(errno) — expect ECONNREFUSED, immediately
Connect to a filtered address and time how long it takes — expect ETIMEDOUT after many seconds
Start a server, connect, kill the server, then write from the client — observe EPIPE or SIGPIPE
Add signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN) and confirm you now get -1 with EPIPE instead of the process dying
Start two copies of your server on the same port without SO_REUSEADDR — expect EADDRINUSE
Set SO_RCVTIMEO to 2 seconds, connect to a server that never replies, and confirm read returns after 2 seconds
Write a client with the backoff loop above and point it at a port that is not listening; watch the delays grow
Remove the jitter, run ten copies at once, and observe that their retries line up
blocks.expected: Each error produced on purpose and identified by name, a SIGPIPE turned into a handleable error by one line, and a retry loop whose delays you can see growing. The last step is worth doing: ten clients retrying in lockstep is a small, visible version of the effect that turns a brief outage into a long one.

cheatsheet: ECONNREFUSED: reachable, nothing listening · ETIMEDOUT: nothing answered at all
ECONNRESET: the peer aborted · EPIPE: you wrote to a closed connection
EADDRINUSE: another instance, or TIME_WAIT without SO_REUSEADDR
EAGAIN and EINTR are NOT errors — handle them as control flow
Retry EINTR immediately, EAGAIN after readiness, ETIMEDOUT with bounded backoff

Never retry EINVAL, EBADF or EACCES — they are bugs or permissions, and repeating them changes nothing. ECONNREFUSED is different: nothing is listening YET, so a bounded backoff is right when you are waiting for a service to come up, and wrong when you have the wrong address
Backoff needs jitter, or every client retries in the same instant
signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN) in every server, or a disconnect kills the process
Every operation needs a timeout — silence produces no error at all
Log the call, the errno name and the peer; capture errno immediately

checkpoint.prompt: Your server dies when a client disconnects mid-response. What is missing?

choices.B: signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN) — writing to a closed connection raises a signal whose default is to terminate

checkpoint.explanation: With it ignored, the write returns -1 with EPIPE and you handle one connection failing. Without it, one client's timing ends the whole process.

checkpoint.prompt: A read fails with EINTR. What should the code do?

choices.A: Close the connection and log an error
choices.B: Retry the call — a signal interrupted it and nothing is wrong

checkpoint.explanation: EINTR and EAGAIN are the two values that are not failures. Treating either as an error produces a program that misbehaves under load, when both become common.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does a retry loop need random jitter?

choices.B: Without it, every client that failed at the same moment retries at the same moment, hitting a struggling service with synchronised waves
choices.D: To make the delays shorter on average

checkpoint.explanation: Backoff alone spreads retries in time but not across clients. The randomness is what desynchronises them, and it is the difference between recovery and an amplified outage.

checkpoint.prompt: A peer accepts your connection and then never responds. What does your program see?

choices.B: Nothing — it waits indefinitely unless you set a timeout

checkpoint.explanation: Silence is the failure with no error. A closed connection is reported; a silent one is not, which is why every operation needs a bound and why long-lived connections send keepalives.
